ety.text: Old French frirebor. Middle English fryen English fry Inherited from Middle English fryen, borrowed from Old French frire, from Latin frīgō. Cognate with Ancient Greek φρύγω (phrúgō, “to roast, bake”), Sanskrit भृज्जति (bhṛjjati, “to roast, grill, fry”). Replaced native Middle English hirsten, from Old English hierstan (“to fry”). Related to bhurji, bhujia (“fried Indian snacks”).

chain.g: spawn of fish, young or small fish, offspring, progeny, children

ety.text: From Middle English frie (“spawn of fish, young or small fish, offspring, progeny, children”), probably from Old Norse frjó (“seed, semen”), from Proto-Germanic *fraiwą (“seed, semen, offspring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per-, *(s)prey- (“to strew, sow”). Cognate with Icelandic frjó (“pollen, seed”), Icelandic fræ (“seed”), Swedish frö (“seed, embryo, grain, germ”), Danish and Norwegian frø (“seed”), Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍅 (fraiw, “seed”). Likely merging with Old French froiz, froie (“spawn, spawning”), from froier, freier (“to spawn”), from Latin fricō (“to rub”). Compare friable.

Dialectal, of obscure origin. Perhaps related to or a corruption of frith (“a wood, forest", also "brushwood, wattle”), from Middle English fryth, frith (“forest, woodland, a fence of brush or wattle, hedge”).

ex: With crackling flames a caldron fries.
Ye might haue seene the frothy billowes fry

senses.d: To suffer because of too much heat.
ex: You'll fry if you go out in this sun with no sunblock on.

senses.d: To execute, or be executed, by the electric chair.
ex: He's guilty of murder: he's going to fry.

senses.d: To destroy (something, usually electronic), often with excessive heat, voltage, or current.
ex: If you apply that much voltage, you'll fry the resistor.
Taking drugs for years fried his brain.

senses.d: To entertain (a person) greatly; to make to laugh thoroughly.
ex: This joke is absolutely frying me.

senses.d: A long, thin fried piece of cut potato.
A long, thin fried piece of other foods.
A meal of fried sausages, bacon, eggs, etc.
A swarm, especially of something small.
A drain, usually made of brushwood.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French fraye (“fry, spawn”), related to frayer. Cognate to Italian frega, fregolo, fregola (“fry, spawn”), Spanish freza (“fry, spawn”). The similarity to English fry and its Germanic family is a coincidence.
